paragraphs.heading: A space built from two spaces
paragraphs.text: Start with V and W, two vector spaces over one shared field. Their tensor product V⊗W is a new vector space, and it comes with a bilinear map that sends each pair (v, w) to an element written v⊗w. That element is called the tensor product of v and w. Any element of V⊗W is called a tensor, and one of the simple form v⊗w is called an elementary or decomposable tensor. Every tensor is a sum of elementary ones.

paragraphs.heading: Bases and dimension
paragraphs.text: If V and W come with bases, pairing each basis element of V with each basis element of W gives a basis of V⊗W. So when V and W are finite-dimensional, V⊗W is too, and its dimension is the product of their two dimensions. Written as a rectangular array, the coordinates of x⊗y are what you get by taking the outer product of the coordinate vector of x with that of y. In this sense the tensor product generalizes the outer product, lifting it beyond coordinate vectors.

paragraphs.heading: A definition using bases
paragraphs.text: One way to define V⊗W picks bases B_V and B_W and declares the symbols v⊗w, with v in B_V and w in B_W, to be a basis, giving them no other meaning. This has drawbacks. Choosing new bases defines a different tensor product, though the two can be identified through a canonical isomorphism. It also cannot be extended to a definition for modules over a ring.

paragraphs.heading: A definition without bases
paragraphs.text: A construction that does not depend on bases begins with a vector space L whose basis is the entire Cartesian product V × W. Each pair (v, w) is then one basis element of L. The result of this construction can be shown to satisfy the universal property below, and a very similar construction gives the tensor product of modules.

paragraphs.heading: The universal property
paragraphs.text: The tensor product can also be pinned down by what it does. It is a vector space V⊗W together with a bilinear map φ sending (v, w) to v⊗w, such that each bilinear map h from V × W into a vector space Z equals h̃∘φ for exactly one linear map h̃ from V⊗W to Z. Any two objects with this property are related by a unique isomorphism, so the tensor product is defined up to isomorphism. The constructions above then serve as proofs that it exists, and every property of it can be deduced from the universal property alone.

paragraphs.heading: Functions and physics
paragraphs.text: Functions give a concrete case. For complex-valued functions f on a set S and g on a set T, f⊗g is the function on S×T that sends (s, t) to f(s)g(t). Tensor products are also used in physics and engineering. In general relativity, gravity is described by the metric tensor, a tensor field that assigns one tensor to each point of space-time, each lying in the tensor product of the cotangent space at that point with itself.
